The ADA development in 30/open-label participants suggests immunogenicity may have compromised drug exposure. The high flare rate in both arms (~80%+) suggests either the population was very high-risk or the prednisone taper itself was insufficient to maintain remission, potentially creating a floor effect. The trial was adequately powered (n=183) and ran for 12 months, so underpowering and wrong timeframe are less likely primary explanations. The primary failure appears to be that the mechanism (T-cell co-stimulation blockade) did not translate to clinical benefit in this SLE population, with additional safety concerns. Multiple factors are at play: the mechanism may be insufficient for SLE (wrong population/mechanism), there are safety signals, and immunogenicity may have reduced drug efficacy.

failure_modes.evidence: No PD biomarker data confirms biology moved; however, the mechanism is plausible and the endpoint clearly missed (HR=1.1). Without pathway biomarker data, we cannot confirm whether biology moved at all.

SLE is a heterogeneous disease with multiple immune pathways. T-cell co-stimulation blockade via CD80/CD86 may be insufficient or not the dominant driver in this unselected SLE flare population. The mechanism works in RA (abatacept is approved) but SLE has additional B-cell, complement, and innate immune components not addressed by this mechanism.

The trial failed due to a combination of: (1) mechanism likely insufficient for SLE (wrong population/mechanism), (2) immunogenicity concerns (ADA in 30 OL participants), (3) higher SAE rate in abatacept arm potentially reflecting disease exacerbation or drug toxicity, and (4) high background flare rate in both arms (~80%) suggesting the prednisone taper design may have created a high-noise environment.
